[2026-15666: lines 105-344 of 4700, FR page 49230]
   105  meaningful administrative review while reducing delay, fragmentation, 
   106  and unnecessary litigation burden.
   107  
   108  I. Digest of Public Comments and Summary of Changes From the Proposed 
   109  Rule
   110  
   111      In response to the proposed rule, OPM received 1,252 comments 
   112  during the 30-day public comment period from a variety of individuals, 
   113  including current and former civil servants, members of Congress, as 
   114  well as organizations, including local and national unions and Federal 
   115  agencies. Of the 1,252 comments, 1,251 were posted on 
   116  www.regulations.gov, and one was not posted because it contained vulgar 
   117  language unrelated to the rulemaking in question. At the conclusion of 
   118  the public comment period, OPM reviewed and analyzed the comments. In 
   119  general, the comments ranged from ardent support of the proposed 
   120  regulation to categorical rejection of it. Less than 1 percent of the 
   121  overall comments were supportive, neutral, or mixed, and 99 percent 
   122  opposed the proposed regulation.
   123      OPM found many of the comments helpful. OPM has revised the final 
   124  rule to clarify, narrow, or supplement the proposed RIF appeal 
   125  procedures in response to comments, including comments concerning 
   126  burden of proof, access to the agency record, information asymmetry, 
   127  due process, neutrality, hearings, protective orders, collective 
   128  bargaining, and public disclosure. In response to those comments, the 
   129  final rule adds more precise appeal standards, a detailed RIF-specific 
   130  agency-record requirement, disclosure and privilege protections, 
   131  stronger adjudicator-separation and ex parte safeguards, narrower e-
   132  filing sanctions, more flexible reply rules, and more carefully 
   133  tailored protective order and public posting provisions. The revisions 
   134  are summarized below.
   135      Clarifying appealable actions. The final text clarifies the 
   136  appealable actions set forth in Sec.  351.901(a). The proposal allowed 
   137  an employee ``who has been the subject of a reduction-in-force action'' 
   138  to appeal an action taken under part 351. The final text specifies that 
   139  only an employee furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, or 
   140  demoted by a RIF action taken under part 351 may appeal that action to 
   141  OPM.
   142      Revising the merits standard. The final text replaces the proposed 
   143  ``would not have suffered the same or another RIF action'' standard in 
   144  Sec.  351.901(b) with a more precise two-part merits showing: the 
   145  appellant must prove that the agency failed to comply with an 
   146  applicable statute or OPM regulation governing RIF actions under part 
   147  351, and the failure prejudiced the appellant by causing the appealed 
   148  action or the loss of a materially more favorable outcome. This is 
   149  clearer and better focused on prejudicial RIF-compliance error.
   150      Revising exclusivity language. The final text continues to provide 
   151  that part 351 procedures are the sole and exclusive means of appealing 
   152  a RIF action, and adds that RIFs and matters related to the appeals of 
   153  RIFs cannot be raised in grievance procedures or challenged through 
   154  grievance arbitration, while expressly preserving collateral matters 
   155  within the independent jurisdiction of Equal Employment Opportunity 
   156  Commission (EEOC), Inspectors General, MSPB, Department of Labor 
   157  Veterans' Employment and Training Service (DOL VETS), and the Office of 
   158  Special Counsel (OSC). The final text also retains the no-judicial-
   159  review provision.
   160      Updating filing-system language. The final text replaces the 
   161  proposed placeholder for the electronic filing system with a reference 
   162  to the system identified on OPM's website. It also replaces 
   163  ``statements, evidence, or documents'' with ``pleadings, evidence, or 
   164  documents,'' better aligning the filing provision with adjudicatory 
   165  terminology.
   166      Clarifying filing deadlines. The final text changes the filing 
   167  deadline from 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time to 11:59 p.m. Eastern 
   168  Time, avoiding confusion during daylight saving time. It also 
   169  consolidates the untimely-filing rule in Sec.  351.902(b)(2) and 
   170  provides that good-cause determinations are within OPM's sole and 
   171  exclusive discretion.
   172      Adding a limited tolling rule for collateral matters. The final 
   173  text adds Sec.  351.902(b)(3), which permits an employee who timely 
   174  filed a collateral matter within the independent jurisdiction of an 
   175  entity identified in Sec.  351.901(c) to file a RIF appeal within 30 
   176  calendar days after the final decision on that matter, where that 
   177  decision materially affects the employee's retention standing, order of 
   178  release, assignment rights, or other rights under part 351. The final 
   179  text provides that a decision is final for this purpose when it is no 
   180  longer subject to further administrative review and that OPM 
   181  determines, in its sole and exclusive discretion, whether the decision 
   182  materially affects the employee's rights.
   183      Requiring filing-information detail in the RIF notice. The final 
   184  text amends Sec.  351.802(a)(6) to require the specific RIF notice to 
   185  state, in addition to the employee's right to appeal to OPM, the
   186  
   187  [[Page 49231]]
   188  
   189  time limit for filing an appeal under Sec.  351.902(b) and the 
   190  electronic filing system through which an appeal must be filed.
   191      Narrowing e-filing enforcement. The final text narrows the proposed 
   192  e-filing enforcement provisions. Rather than authorizing broader orders 
   193  regulating filing methods, sanctions, misuse, or termination of e-filer 
   194  participation, the final text provides that OPM may strike a document 
   195  when an e-filer repeatedly fails to follow filing instructions after a 
   196  show-cause order. The final text also removes the proposed statement 
   197  that withdrawal from e-filing may preclude future re-registration and 
   198  clarifies that withdrawal of e-filing registration is not good cause 
   199  for staying a case.
   200      Simplifying initial-appeal information. The final text simplifies 
   201  the contact-information requirements in Sec.  351.903(a) by replacing 
   202  ``legal name, best address'' with ``name, address.'' The core 
   203  requirement remains unchanged: the appeal must be written, state the 
   204  basis for the appeal, identify the appellant and any representative, 
   205  and include supporting documentation.
   206      Defining the agency record. The final text adds a RIF-specific 
   207  minimum agency-record requirement to Sec.  351.903(b). The proposal 
   208  required the agency response to include the agency record but did not 
   209  define its contents. The final text specifies that the agency record 
   210  includes, at a minimum, the RIF notice and effective-date documents, 
   211  documents supporting the RIF reason, coverage and appointment records, 
   212  competitive-area and competitive-level records, retention-register and 
   213  retention-standing records, order-of-release records, assignment-rights 
   214  records, special RIF-circumstance records, and a certification that the 
   215  complete agency record has been produced.
   216      Distinguishing production to OPM from service on the appellant. The 
   217  final text requires the agency to produce the complete agency record to 
   218  OPM while serving the appellant with the agency record subject to 
   219  legally required limits. The agency may redact or withhold information 
   220  from the appellant's copy only to the extent necessary to comply with 
   221  the Privacy Act, applicable legal privileges, classified-information or 
   222  national-security requirements, OPM protective orders, or other 
   223  disclosure limits required by law.
   224      Allowing limited new matters in reply. The final text revises Sec.  
   225  351.903(c) to permit an appellant's reply to raise a new allegation of 
   226  error if the basis for that allegation rests on information first 
   227  disclosed in the agency response or if OPM grants leave for good cause.
   228      Adding disclosure limits for inspection and service. The final text 
   229  makes inspection of OPM's appellate record and service of documents 
   230  subject to the Privacy Act, applicable legal privileges, classified-
   231  information or national-security requirements, OPM protective orders, 
   232  and other applicable disclosure limits required by law. The proposal 
   233  allowed inspection and required service but did not include the same 
   234  express disclosure limitations.
   235      Reorganizing representative provisions. The final text reorganizes 
   236  Sec.  351.904 into separate paragraphs addressing designation of a 
   237  representative, Federal employee representatives and restrictions on 
   238  official time and reimbursement, and disallowance of representatives. 
   239  The final text also narrows the grounds for disallowing a 
   240  representative. Because a Federal employee representative may not 
   241  perform representational functions while in a duty status, the final 
   242  text does not adopt the proposed additional grounds for disallowance 
   243  based on the priority needs of the Government or unreasonable costs to 
   244  the Government; OPM or the responsible agency may disallow an 
   245  employee's choice of representative only where the representative is an 
   246  employee of the responsible agency or OPM and the representative's 
   247  activities would cause a conflict of interest or position. The 
   248  remaining changes are primarily organizational and clarifying.
   249      Adding adjudicator-separation and ex parte safeguards. The final 
   250  text adds safeguards in Sec.  351.905(a) requiring OPM adjudicators to 
   251  be insulated from officials who participated personally and 
   252  substantially in the challenged action or provided case-specific 
   253  advice. It also prohibits adjudicators from considering material ex 
   254  parte communications on the merits and requires any such communication 
   255  to be summarized in the record with an opportunity for party response, 
   256  unless disclosure is prohibited by law.
   257      Clarifying OPM employee appeals. The final text clarifies that an 
   258  administrative law judge (ALJ) assigned to adjudicate an OPM employee's 
   259  appeal will issue an initial decision. It also adds material factual 
   260  error affecting the outcome as a ground on which OPM may disturb the 
   261  ALJ's decision and clarifies that assigning an ALJ does not make 5 
   262  U.S.C. 554, 556, or 557 applicable unless independently required by law 
   263  or expressly incorporated.
   264      Tightening audits and investigations. The final text narrows the 
   265  standard for OPM audits or investigations. The proposal allowed OPM to 
   266  conduct an audit or investigation when the ``interest of justice'' 
   267  would be served. The final text requires OPM to determine that the 
   268  existing record is insufficient to resolve a material issue within 
   269  OPM's jurisdiction and that the audit or investigation is reasonably 
   270  likely to produce material information. The final text also provides 
   271  that representatives may not participate in an audit or investigation 
   272  unless OPM specifically requests it.
   273      Removing a separate ascertainment sanction. The final text removes 
   274  the proposed separate paragraph authorizing sanctions for failure to 
   275  participate in ascertainment of facts and renumbers the initial-
   276  decision and remedies provisions.
   277      Refining protective-order authority. The final text revises Sec.  
   278  351.906(a). The proposal focused on harassing communications and use of 
   279  appeal information for unrelated purposes. The final text authorizes 
   280  protective orders or cease-and-desist directives to protect the 
   281  integrity of the adjudicatory process and to prevent threats, 
   282  intimidation, targeted harassment, improper witness contact, disclosure 
   283  of protected personal information, or misuse of nonpublic information 
   284  obtained through the appeal. It also requires protective orders to be 
   285  no broader than reasonably necessary and not to restrict lawful 
   286  communications protected by law.
   287      Clarifying OPM-initiated reconsideration. The final text clarifies 
   288  in Sec.  351.907(a) that OPM may reopen and reconsider an initial 
   289  decision either upon request of a party or on its own initiative. The 
   290  proposal allowed party-requested reconsideration, while Director sua 
   291  sponte review was addressed separately.
   292      Clarifying Director review. The final text revises Sec.  351.908 to 
   293  preserve the Director's sua sponte authority to reopen and reconsider a 
   294  nonfinal initial decision or reopened and reconsidered decision, while 
   295  identifying nonexclusive considerations that may guide that review. The 
   296  proposal gave the Director broad discretion to reopen and reconsider 
   297  any nonfinal decision. The final text clarifies that the Director may 
   298  consider whether the decision contains clear legal error, rests on an 
   299  erroneous material factual finding, involves an issue of exceptional 
   300  importance, affects governmentwide civil service administration, 
   301  conflicts with another OPM decision, or otherwise warrants review. It 
   302  also clarifies that Sec.  351.908 does not create a party right to 
   303  request Director review and that, upon reopening, the Director may take 
   304  any action available under Sec.  351.907(c).

   306  [[Page 49232]]
   307  
   308      Revising finality of initial decisions. The final text revises 
   309  Sec.  351.909 so that an initial decision becomes final 30 calendar 
   310  days after issuance unless, before that time, a party timely requests 
   311  reopening and reconsideration under Sec.  351.907 or the Director 
   312  reopens the decision under Sec.  351.908. A timely request suspends 
   313  finality: if OPM denies or dismisses the request without reopening the 
   314  initial decision, the initial decision becomes final 30 calendar days

   316  it before that time, and if OPM grants the request, the reopened and

   318  unless the Director reopens that decision before that time. An untimely 
   319  request does not suspend or otherwise affect finality. The final text

   322  remands the appeal or directs further proceedings, any resulting 
   323  decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909. These changes conform 
   324  finality to the reconsideration and Director-review provisions of the

Note Q7(b): appeal to OPM, e-filing via OPM website; 30 calendar days from effective date of action (Dec 18, 2026). Counting: first day counted is day after effective date = Dec 19. 30th calendar day after Dec 18 = Jan 17, 2027. Dec 19 is day 1 → Dec 31 is day 13 → Jan 17 is day 30 (Dec has 31 days: days 1-13 = Dec 19-31; Jan 1 = day 14; Jan 17 = day 30). So last day Jan 17, 2027, which is a Sunday → next workday Monday Jan 18, 2027 — but Jan 18, 2027 is Martin Luther King Jr. Day (third Monday in January 2027: Jan 4 is Monday? Let's compute: Jan 1, 2027 is a Friday. So Mondays: Jan 4, 11, 18, 25. Third Monday = Jan 18 → Federal holiday). So the filing period includes the first workday after — Tuesday, January 19, 2027, 11:59 p.m. ET. 

Wait — let me verify the day of the week for Dec 18, 2026 (given as Friday in the scenario). Dec 18, 2026 Friday. Then Jan 1, 2027: Dec 18 + 14 = Jan 1 → Friday + 14 days = Friday. Yes, Jan 1, 2027 is a Friday. Jan 17 = Sunday (Jan 1 Fri, Jan 8 Fri, Jan 15 Fri, Jan 17 Sun). Yes. Jan 18 Monday = MLK Day. So first workday after = Tuesday Jan 19, 2027.

Q7(a): Notice Aug 31, 2026 (before Sept 2) → old rules apply (DATES of 2026-15666: applies only to RIF action for which agency issues specific RIF notice on or after Sept 2, 2026). So MSPB hears the appeal. Which 2026 documents bear on it: 2026-15666 (its DATES limiting prospective application), 2026-17338 correction (effective Sept 2), and MSPB's Appellate Jurisdiction Update II 2026-16456 (effective Sept 2) — presumably it addresses RIF appeals where notice issued before Sept 2 (retaining jurisdiction over those). Need to read 2026-16456.

Q7(e): 351.901(c)(4): "A party cannot obtain judicial review of a decision under this subpart." → No.

Q7(f): 351.902(b)(3): timely collateral OSC complaint filed before expiration of filing period; final decision Mar 10, 2027 materially affects retention standing → may file appeal within 30 calendar days after the decision becomes final and no longer subject to further administrative review. So yes, if the March 10, 2027 decision is final and not subject to further administrative review; deadline 30 calendar days after that date → April 9, 2027. Compute: Mar 10 + 30 days = April 9, 2027. Also note: OSC's final decision — is it subject to further review? OSC decisions: the employee may seek review... Hmm. The scenario says "final decision correcting the rating". So deadline: 30 calendar days after the date the decision becomes final; if it became final on March 10, 2027, then April 9, 2027. Need to mention "and no longer subject to further administrative review". Also is April 9, 2027 a Friday? Apr 9, 2027: Jan 1 Fri; Apr 9... let's not bother but check: April 9, 2027 — 2027 Jan 1 Friday. Days to Apr 9 = 98 days (Jan 31, Feb 28, Mar 31 = 90; Apr 9 = day 99). 99 mod 7 = 1 (since day 1 = Friday), day 99 → 98 days after → 98 mod 7 = 0 → Friday. So April 9, 2027 is a Friday. Good.

Q7(c): burden of proof: preponderance on timeliness, jurisdiction, failure to comply with statute/OPM regulation, and prejudice (351.901(b)). Hearing: not entitled; record-based review unless OPM determines a hearing is necessary and efficient (351.905(c)).

Q7(d): 351.901(c)(2): RIF action and matters relating to appeal may not be raised under negotiated grievance procedure or grievance arbitration. Preamble on existing CBAs — need to read section I (1828-2027). Let me read that plus the judicial review section (1579-1742) and scope of RIF appeals/collateral claims (1742-1828).

  1730  is unavailable informs the public of the operative legal parameters.

  1733  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1734  
  1735      \23\ See Elgin v. Dep't of Treasury, 567 U.S. 1, 11-12 (2012); 
  1736  Grosdidier v. Chair. of Broad. Bd. of Governors, 560 F.3d 495, 497

  1738  (D.C. Cir. 2009); Graham v. Ashcroft, 358 F.3d 931, 935 (D.C. Cir. 
  1739  2004); Fornaro v. James, 416 F.3d 63, 67 (D.C. Cir. 2005).
  1740  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1741  
  1742  H. Scope of RIF Appeals and Collateral Claims
  1743  
  1744      Commenters 0370, 0928, 0962, 1025, 1089, 1092, 1099, 1165, and 1217 
  1745  raised concerns about the scope of OPM review and the preservation of 
  1746  collateral claims. Commenters argued that the proposal could weaken 
  1747  civil-rights enforcement, eliminate mixed-case processing, prevent 
  1748  employees from raising pretext or retaliation, or force employees into 
  1749  multiple forums. Commenters 0046, 0074, 0540, and 1252 contended that 
  1750  the rule would eliminate the ability to appeal discrimination claims in 
  1751  connection with RIFs entirely and allow agencies to RIF employees in 
  1752  protected classes with impunity.
  1753      The final rule clarifies the scope of OPM's review. OPM will 
  1754  adjudicate whether the agency failed to comply with an applicable 
  1755  statute or OPM regulation governing RIF actions under part 351 and 
  1756  whether that failure prejudiced the appellant. This includes RIF-
  1757  compliance issues such as coverage, competitive area, competitive 
  1758  level, retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, notice, 
  1759  special RIF circumstances, and related requirements.
  1760      At the same time, the final rule preserves collateral statutory 
  1761  avenues. Final Sec.  351.901(c) states that the procedures in part 351 
  1762  are the sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action, but do not 
  1763  otherwise preclude an employee from filing a complaint, appeal, or 
  1764  other matter within the jurisdiction of EEOC, an Inspector General, 
  1765  MSPB, DOL VETS, or OSC. This provision reflects OPM's intent to channel 
  1766  direct challenges to RIF compliance through OPM while preserving 
  1767  matters Congress or applicable law has assigned to other forums.
  1768      OPM acknowledges that some claims previously could have been 
  1769  combined with a RIF appeal before MSPB because OPM's regulation made 
  1770  RIF actions appealable to MSPB. That prior combined forum was a 
  1771  consequence of OPM's regulatory delegation to MSPB, not an independent 
  1772  statutory requirement that OPM retain MSPB jurisdiction. The final rule 
  1773  preserves the substantive availability of discrimination, 
  1774  whistleblower, veterans' rights, prohibited-personnel-practice, and 
  1775  Inspector General matters in the proper forums.
  1776      Commenter 0463 asserted that the exclusive RIF appeal procedure 
  1777  could abrogate or supersede appeal rights available to preference 
  1778  eligible veterans under 5 U.S.C. 3330a and 3330b. OPM disagrees. The 
  1779  final rule's exclusivity provision governs direct appeals of RIF 
  1780  actions under part 351; it does not displace independent statutory 
  1781  causes of action that Congress assigned to other forums. Final Sec.  
  1782  351.901(c) expressly preserves an employee's ability to file a 
  1783  complaint, appeal, or other matter within the jurisdiction of, among 
  1784  others, MSPB and the Department of Labor Veterans' Employment and 
  1785  Training Service. That preservation language includes claims under the 
  1786  Veterans Employment Opportunities Act. Under 5 U.S.C. 3330a, a 
  1787  preference eligible who alleges that an agency violated the 
  1788  individual's rights under a statute or regulation relating to veterans' 
  1789  preference may file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor, and, if 
  1790  the matter is not resolved, may appeal to MSPB under the procedures 
  1791  Congress specified. 5 U.S.C. 3330a. Section 3330b separately provides 
  1792  for judicial redress in district court in lieu of continuing the 
  1793  administrative redress procedure after the statutory prerequisites are 
  1794  met. 5 U.S.C. 3330b. Nothing in this final rule alters those statutory 
  1795  rights, filing deadlines, forum assignments, or judicial-redress 
  1796  provisions.
  1797      The final rule also reinforces, rather than weakens, the ability to 
  1798  identify and address veterans' preference issues in a RIF appeal. 
  1799  Section 351.903(b) requires the agency record to include documents 
  1800  establishing the appellant's veterans' preference status and related 
  1801  retention information, including records supporting veterans' 
  1802  preference credit, tenure subgroup, service computation date, the 
  1803  retention register, order of release, assignment rights, and any 
  1804  special RIF circumstance relevant to the appellant. Thus, where the 
  1805  issue is whether the agency complied with part 351's RIF requirements 
  1806  as applied to a preference eligible, OPM will have the relevant RIF 
  1807  record before it. Where the issue is an independent veterans' 
  1808  preference claim under 5 U.S.C. 3330a
  1809  
  1810  [[Page 49244]]
  1811  
  1812  or 3330b, the final rule leaves that statutory route undisturbed.
  1813      Commenter 0074 similarly asserted that the revised RIF appeal 
  1814  procedure would allow agencies to engage in pretextual terminations of 
  1815  employees with disabilities in violation of the Rehabilitation Act of 
  1816  1973. OPM disagrees. The final rule does not authorize agencies to use 
  1817  RIF procedures as a pretext for disability discrimination or any other 
  1818  unlawful personnel practice. Federal employees and applicants remain 
  1819  protected by section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act, 29 U.S.C. 791, and 
  1820  the remedies, procedures, and rights available under 29 U.S.C. 794a, 
  1821  including the Federal-sector procedures incorporated from Title VII. In 
  1822  addition, disability discrimination remains a prohibited personnel 
  1823  practice under 5 U.S.C. 2302(b)(1)(D). The final rule expressly 
  1824  preserves matters within the jurisdiction of the EEOC and OSC and 
  1825  therefore does not redirect Rehabilitation Act claims into OPM's RIF 
  1826  appeal process or limit the remedies available under those statutes.
  1827  
  1828  I. Collective Bargaining, Grievance Arbitration, and CBAs
  1829  
  1830      Commenters 0962, 1025, 1092, 0928, and 1217 objected to the 
  1831  proposal's treatment of negotiated grievance procedures, arbitration, 
  1832  and collective bargaining agreements. These commenters argued that the 
  1833  Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute protects negotiated 
  1834  grievance and arbitration procedures; that RIF matters are not among 
  1835  the matters excluded from negotiated grievance procedures under 5 
  1836  U.S.C. 7121(c); that questions of arbitrability should be resolved 
  1837  through negotiated grievance procedures; and that OPM may not use a 
  1838  governmentwide regulation to eliminate existing collective-bargaining 
  1839  rights or union representation. Other commenters, including 0221, 0584, 
  1840  0587, 0591, and 0621, asserted that the proposal would unlawfully 
  1841  supersede existing CBAs, while commenters 0386 and 1004 requested a 
  1842  clearer legal basis for OPM's position. Commenters 0049, 0092, 0483, 
  1843  and others objected as a policy matter to any prospective limitation on 
  1844  negotiated RIF appeal procedures.
  1845      OPM has considered these comments and has decided to finalize the 
  1846  regulatory text as initially proposed, with some modifications. The 
  1847  final Sec.  351.901(c) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  1848  ``sole and exclusive means'' of appealing a RIF action, and matters 
  1849  relating to such actions may not be raised under a negotiated grievance 
  1850  procedure or contested through grievance arbitration, but employees are 
  1851  not otherwise impeded from filing a complaint, appeal, or other matter 
  1852  within the jurisdiction of the EEOC, an Inspector General, MSPB, DOL 
  1853  VETS, or OSC.
  1854      OPM continues to conclude that a single governmentwide process for 
  1855  direct RIF-compliance appeals is necessary to ensure uniform 
  1856  interpretation and application of part 351. RIF appeals under part 351 
  1857  involve governmentwide rules governing competitive areas, competitive 
  1858  levels, retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, 
  1859  notice, and related requirements. Allowing agencies to create or 
  1860  bargain for parallel direct appeal mechanisms for the same RIF-
  1861  compliance claim would undermine the consistency, finality, and 
  1862  efficiency the final rule is designed to achieve.
  1863      This conclusion is consistent with 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). That 
  1864  provision states that the duty to bargain extends only ``to the extent 
  1865  not inconsistent with any Federal law or any governmentwide rule or 
  1866  regulation,'' and, for matters that are the subject of a rule or 
  1867  regulation, applies only where the rule or regulation is not 
  1868  governmentwide. 5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1). This final rule is a 
  1869  governmentwide regulation: it applies across agencies to appeals of 
  1870  covered RIF actions under part 351. To that end, it firmly and 
  1871  completely limits the flexibility of agencies to provide processes not 
  1872  contemplated by this rule, including grievance arbitration. See U.S. 
  1873  Dep't of Treasury, I.R.S. v. FLRA, 996 F.2d 1246, 1250 (D.C. Cir. 1993) 
  1874  (IRS) (5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1) ``permits the government to pull a subject 
  1875  out of the bargaining process by issuing a governmentwide rule that 
  1876  creates a regime inconsistent with bargaining,'' including where a 
  1877  regulation ``sets out an exclusive method of resolving any claims''). 
  1878  Accordingly, agencies may not bargain for a claims-channeling process 
  1879  that conflicts with the final rule's designation of part 351 as the 
  1880  sole and exclusive means of directly appealing a RIF action.
  1881      OPM is not persuaded by commenters' argument that 5 U.S.C. 
  1882  7121(a)(1) overrides this conclusion. Section 7121(a)(1) requires CBAs 
  1883  to provide procedures for settlement of grievances, including questions 
  1884  of arbitrability, and makes those procedures the exclusive 
  1885  administrative procedures for grievances that fall within their 
  1886  coverage. But that provision must be read together with section 
  1887  7117(a)(1), which limits the duty to bargain where the matter is 
  1888  inconsistent with Federal law or a governmentwide rule or regulation. 
  1889  The broad definition of ``grievance'' in 5 U.S.C. 7103(a)(9) likewise 
  1890  does not displace section 7117(a)(1). The fact that RIFs are not listed 
  1891  in section 7121(c) does not mean parties may bargain for an alternative 
  1892  direct RIF appeal procedure that conflicts with a governmentwide 
  1893  regulation establishing a single appeal process.
  1894      The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeal's decision in IRS addressed 
  1895  exactly this issue. The court held that a union proposal that would 
  1896  permit grievances over contracting out was non-negotiable as it 
  1897  conflicted with OMB Circular A-76, a government-wide rule that 
  1898  prescribed the exclusive method for resolving disputes over contracting 
  1899  decisions. The court thus held that Circular A-76 prohibited bargaining 
  1900  over conflicting appeals processes. The final Sec.  351.901(c) 
  1901  similarly prohibits creating an alternative RIF appeals process through 
  1902  collective bargaining.
  1903      OPM also disagrees with Commenter 0962's assertion that section 
  1904  7121(a)(1) has primacy over section 7117(a)(1). Sections 7103, 7117, 
  1905  and 7121 are part of the same statutory scheme and must be read 
  1906  together. Section 7121 establishes negotiated grievance procedures for 
  1907  matters properly within a CBA's coverage; section 7117(a)(1) defines 
  1908  the outer boundary of the bargaining obligation where Federal law or a 
  1909  governmentwide regulation has occupied the field. Reading section 7121 
  1910  to require negotiated grievance arbitration of direct RIF appeals 
  1911  notwithstanding section 7117 would effectively nullify section 
  1912  7117(a)(1) for any matter that could be characterized as a grievance. 
  1913  In IRS the D.C. Circuit expressly rejected that statutory construction. 
  1914  OPM accordingly declines to adopt that reading.
  1915      Nor is this final rule merely a restatement of management rights 
  1916  under 5 U.S.C. 7106. Section 7106 preserves agency authority, subject 
  1917  to subsection (b), to determine mission, budget, organization, number 
  1918  of employees, internal security practices, and to lay off and retain 
  1919  employees, while also preserving bargaining over procedures and 
  1920  appropriate arrangements in appropriate circumstances. 5 U.S.C. 
  1921  7106(a), (b). The final rule does not simply repeat those management 
  1922  rights. It establishes a detailed governmentwide appellate process 
  1923  governing who may appeal, the burden of proof, filing deadlines, 
  1924  agency-record production, service, replies, inspection of the appellate 
  1925  record, representation, adjudication, protective orders, 
  1926  reconsideration, Director review, and finality.
  1927  
  1928  [[Page 49245]]
  1929  
  1930      For that reason, commenters' reliance on Office of Personnel 
  1931  Management v. FLRA, 864 F.2d 165 (D.C. Cir. 1988), is misplaced. In 
  1932  that case, the court addressed whether a governmentwide regulation that 
  1933  merely restated management rights could displace bargaining 
  1934  obligations. This rule does not merely restate a management right; it 
  1935  creates a specific, comprehensive appeal procedure for covered RIF 
  1936  actions. The final rule is therefore more closely aligned with the 
  1937  principle that a governmentwide rule may establish an exclusive method 
  1938  for resolving a particular category of claims, rather than simply 
  1939  invoking management rights at a high level of generality.
  1940      OPM also considered comments invoking the general purposes of the 
  1941  FSLMRS, including 5 U.S.C. 7101(a)(1), which recognizes that collective 
  1942  bargaining safeguards the public interest, contributes to the effective 
  1943  conduct of public business, and facilitates amicable dispute 
  1944  resolution. OPM does not dispute those principles. But section 7101 
  1945  must be read with the rest of chapter 71, including section 7117(a)(1), 
  1946  and with section 7101(b)'s direction that chapter 71 be interpreted 
  1947  consistently with the requirements of an effective and efficient 
  1948  Government. Those provisions support, rather than preclude, a 
  1949  governmentwide rule establishing one uniform process for direct RIF-
  1950  compliance appeals and prohibiting grievances over matters pertaining 
  1951  to RIF appeals.
  1952      In addition to the benefits of maintaining a uniform process for 
  1953  direct RIF-compliance appeals, OPM believes it is beneficial to 
  1954  foreclose grievance arbitration in particular as a forum for 
  1955  adjudicating RIF appeals. As OPM explained in the proposed rule, the 
  1956  arbitrators who adjudicate Federal-sector grievances are private 
  1957  contractors who typically do not have a background in agency operations 
  1958  or Federal employment law. This makes them ill-suited to evaluate 
  1959  potentially complex issues involved in arbitration appeals. OPM is 
  1960  aware of multiple studies showing that, across multiple 
  1961  administrations, the FLRA overturns arbitral awards at a high rate.\24\ 
  1962  The author of one of these studies, himself an arbitrator, concluded 
  1963  that ``Federal sector arbitration is more complex than private sector 
  1964  arbitration. The federal field is full of land mines in the form of 
  1965  laws with which federal sector arbitrators may be less familiar.'' \25\ 
  1966  Foreclosing grievance arbitration ensures adjudication will be handled 
  1967  by MSAC employees with specialized legal and subject matter expertise 
  1968  who are less likely to make reversible errors.
  1969  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1970  
  1971      \24\ See James Sherk, ``Federal Union Arbitrators Frequently 
  1972  Misapply the Law,'' (Aug. 2, 2023), https://www.americafirstpolicy.com/issues/expert-insight-federal-union-arbitrators-frequently-misapply-the-law (finding that between 2019 
  1973  and 2023 over 40 percent of arbitration awards were overturned or 
  1974  remanded upon appeal); see also Helburn, B. (2019). The Trump FLRA: 
  1975  Fair or foul (Helburn), at 6. https://cdn.govexec.com/media/gbc/docs/pdfs_edit/060619ew1.pdf (finding the FLRA set aside or remanded 
  1976  arbitration awards 80, 50, and 43 percent of the time in a sampling 
  1977  of cases arising under the Trump 45, Obama, and George W. Bush 
  1978  Administrations, respectively).
  1979      \25\ Helburn at 10.
  1980  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1981  
  1982      Additionally, under 5 U.S.C. 7122(a) arbitral awards concerning RIF 
  1983  appeals are subject to FLRA review. This review can be protracted, 
  1984  especially if the FLRA loses a quorum or the FLRA has a vacancy and the 
  1985  remaining members deadlock.\26\ Authorizing grievance arbitration over 
  1986  RIF actions would thus create a protracted second level of appeals that 
  1987  would undermine the expeditious resolution of cases. OPM declines to 
  1988  adopt this approach.
  1989  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

content.text:
Key Q14(i) material: correction changes 351.901(c)(1) from "procedures in this part" to "procedures in this subpart" — and the preamble repeatedly says part 351 procedures are the "sole and exclusive means" (e.g., lines 150-159, 1847-1850, which describe as "part 351 procedures"). Hmm, that's a preamble/text difference introduced by the correction: preamble says part 351 is sole and exclusive; corrected text says "this subpart" (subpart I). That's one item.

Also the correction says the document contained "an imprecise cross-reference in Sec. 351.902(b)(3)" — the final rule's own digest (line 172-182) describes 351.902(b)(3) as referring to "an entity identified in Sec. 351.901(c)" while corrected text refers to 351.901(c)(3). That's a preamble (FR 49230) vs corrected text (FR 54796) difference? Hmm, that's arguably a preamble statement that differs from corrected text. But is it "about what the rule provides"? Marginal. Careful: Q14(i) asks for preamble statements about what the rule provides that differ from its regulatory text as published or as corrected. Candidates:
1. Preamble (49230, digest "Revising exclusivity language") says "the final text continues to provide that part 351 procedures are the sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action" vs corrected 351.901(c)(1) "procedures in this subpart". Also 1847-1850 says "the procedures in part 351 are the 'sole and exclusive means'". And 1761-1762 says "the procedures in part 351 are the sole and exclusive means".
   Note also as published the text said "this part" matching preamble; the correction changed it to "this subpart", creating the mismatch. Good item with both FR pages (49230/49244 vs 54796).
2. Maybe preamble says employees may appeal furlough >30 days etc. — matches.
3. Preamble statement about "no-judicial-review provision" retained — text has (c)(4). Fine.
4. Anything about the tolling rule? The digest says "permits an employee who timely filed a collateral matter ... to file a RIF appeal within 30 calendar days after the final decision" — text (b)(3) says "If, before the expiration of the filing period in this paragraph (b), the employee timely filed a complaint..." matches.
5. Preamble in section-by-section on 351.901 or 351.902 may have statements; need to read section-by-section (2349-3032). That's ~680 lines. Hmm, that's big but needed for Q14(i). Maybe grep targeted phrases in that range instead.

Also Q14(ii): change from proposal to final not acknowledged in the digest. The digest seems thorough. Need to compare the proposal's regulatory text with the final's. Let me fetch the proposal 2026-02576's regulatory text (subpart I) and compare. Possible unnoticed changes: e.g., 351.901(a) appealable actions; burden; 351.902(b) time limits; 351.905; 351.907; 351.909. Also possibly a change in 351.802(a)(6) or 351.807(e) — the digest mentions 351.802(a)(6). 351.807(e) revision ("An agency determination of eligibility for certification may not be appealed") — was that in the proposal? The digest doesn't mention 351.807(e). If the proposal didn't amend 351.807(e), then that's an unacknowledged change. Let me check the proposal's ToC/amendatory instructions.

Let me get the proposal's TOC.

  1914  burden of proof to demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence:
  1915      (1) The timeliness of the appeal,
  1916      (2) OPM possesses jurisdiction over the appeal, and
  1917      (3) The reduction-in-force action (i.e., more than 30-day furlough, 
  1918  separation, or demotion due to a reduction in force) was conducted 
  1919  inconsistent with either statute or OPM regulations such that the

  1921  action.

  1923  sole and exclusive means of appealing any reduction-in-force action, 
  1924  and shall supersede any appeal procedures found in agency policies or 
  1925  collective bargaining agreements, but they do not otherwise preclude an 
  1926  employee from filing a complaint, appeal, or other matter within the 
  1927  jurisdiction of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, Federal 
  1928  Labor Relations Authority, an Inspector General, Merit Systems 
  1929  Protection Board, the Department of Labor Veterans' Employment and

  1941  statements, evidence, or documents via electronic mail or postal mail.
  1942      (b) Time limits. An employee may submit an appeal of a reduction in

  1944  action. An appeal is deemed timely when it is electronically filed by 
  1945  11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on the 30th calendar day after the

  1947      (1) In computing the number of days allowed for filing an appeal, 
  1948  the first day counted is the day after the effective date of an Agency

  2070  
  2071      (a) Appeals by non-OPM employees. OPM will assign personnel to

  2073  other than OPM. However, no OPM employee may be assigned to adjudicate

  2158  
  2159      (a) Upon a request from either party to the dispute, OPM may, in

content.text:
Now Q14(ii): differences between proposed and final text not acknowledged in the digest. Let me list changes:

1. Proposed 351.901(c): "shall supersede any appeal procedures found in agency policies or collective bargaining agreements" + preserves EEOC, FLRA, IG, MSPB, DOL VETS, OSC. Final: drops FLRA from the list; adds "may not be raised under a negotiated grievance procedure or contested through grievance arbitration"; and splits judicial review into (c)(4) with "a party cannot obtain judicial review of a decision under this subpart". The digest acknowledged "Revising exclusivity language" — mentions adding grievance/arbitration bar and preserving collateral matters, and "retains the no-judicial-review provision." Does it acknowledge removing FLRA from the list of entities whose independent jurisdiction is preserved? The digest says "preserving collateral matters within the independent jurisdiction of EEOC, IGs, MSPB, DOL VETS, and OSC" — it lists entities but doesn't flag removal of FLRA. Hmm, is that "not acknowledged"? The digest's list omits FLRA. Arguably it's acknowledged implicitly? Risky. But it's a real difference: FLRA dropped. Actually the elimination of FLRA may be implied by the arbitration bar. I'd list cautiously with explanation quoting both.

2. Proposed 351.901(b)(3) vs final (b)(3)+(4) — acknowledged ("Revising the merits standard").

3. Proposed 351.902(b)(2)-(3): good cause in (b)(2), determination in (b)(3) separately; final consolidates — acknowledged ("consolidates the untimely-filing rule in 351.902(b)(2)").

4. 351.902(c)(2): final adds "or exempted under paragraph (c)(7) of this section for good cause" — is that acknowledged? Not mentioned in digest. Hmm, the digest mentions "Narrowing e-filing enforcement" and "removes the proposed statement that withdrawal from e-filing may preclude future re-registration and clarifies that withdrawal...not good cause". The addition of the exemption cross-reference in (c)(2) is a substantive change (allows unregistered access if exempted) — not acknowledged. Candidate.

5. 351.903(a): changes acknowledged ("legal name, best address"→"name, address").

6. 351.903(b): restructuring + record definition — acknowledged.

7. 351.903(c) reply — acknowledged.

8. 351.904 — acknowledged (reorganization + narrowing grounds).

9. 351.905(a) — acknowledged. Note also final adds "OPM may assign an administrative law judge" vs proposal "appoint" — minor.

10. 351.905(b): final adds "material factual error that affected the outcome" — acknowledged ("adds material factual error affecting the outcome as a ground"). Final also adds sentence about 5 U.S.C. 554/556/557 — acknowledged ("clarifies that assigning an ALJ does not make 5 U.S.C. 554, 556, or 557 applicable").

11. 351.905(c): narrowing audit standard acknowledged. Also final adds "OPM may require either party to provide additional information" and "may... investigate"; final adds "reasonably likely to produce information material to resolving that issue"; adds "An individual serving as a representative of either party may not participate in an audit or investigation unless OPM specifically requests" — acknowledged. Final also removed "or any other appropriate action" language and "directs the parties to participate in such hearing or comply with such action" — Hmm: proposal: "unless OPM determines that a hearing or any other appropriate action is necessary and efficient to resolve an appeal and directs the parties to participate in such hearing or comply with such action." Final: "unless OPM determines that a hearing is necessary and efficient in resolving an appeal." The digest doesn't mention removing "any other appropriate action". Candidate (moderate).

12. Proposed 351.905(d) "Failure to participate in ascertainment of facts" removed — acknowledged ("Removing a separate ascertainment sanction").

13. 351.906(a) — acknowledged. 351.906(b) "shall" → "may" — not acknowledged? Proposal (b): "OPM shall, except when prohibited by law: (1)...". Final: "OPM may, except when prohibited by law:". That's a real substantive change (mandatory → discretionary) not mentioned in the digest. Candidate! Also final adds (c) scope of sanctions (proportionality) — not acknowledged. Candidate.

14. 351.907(a): acknowledged (OPM-initiated reconsideration).

15. 351.908: acknowledged.

16. 351.909: acknowledged broadly. But note proposed (a) "initial decision becomes the final decision of OPM if a party does not request reopening within 30 calendar days from the date of the initial decision" vs final (a) "30 calendar days after issuance" plus Director reopening. Acknowledged. Proposed (e) public website: final adds disclosure limits — acknowledged.

17. 351.907(a): proposal "within 30 calendar days from issuance of the initial decision" final same. OK.

18. Proposed (c)(7)? fine.

19. Final 351.902(a): "reconsideration of an initial decision" vs proposal "reconsideration of an initial appeal"; "statements"→"pleadings" acknowledged.

20. Final 351.901(c)(1) "The procedures in this part are the sole and exclusive means of appealing a reduction-in-force action taken under this part" vs proposal "any reduction-in-force action" — narrowing to "taken under this part". Partially acknowledged? The digest's "Revising exclusivity language" says "continues to provide that part 351 procedures are the sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action". Not flagging "taken under this part" — minor.

21. Final 351.902(b)(1): "the first day counted is the day after the effective date of an agency action" - same as proposal.

22. Important: proposed 351.901(a) allowed appeal by "employee who has been the subject of a reduction-in-force action" — acknowledged.

23. Proposed 351.802(a)(6): "The employee's right, as applicable, to appeal to OPM. The agency must also comply with Sec. 1201.21 of this title." Final: detailed content requirement. Digest says: "Requiring filing-information detail in the RIF notice. The final text amends Sec. 351.802(a)(6) to require..." — acknowledges. But does it acknowledge removal of the reference to 5 CFR 1201.21? It says "in addition to the employee's right to appeal to OPM, the time limit ... and the electronic filing system". Doesn't mention removing 1201.21 reference. Marginal.

24. 351.807(e): same in both. Fine.

25. Final 351.904 heading structure: "Employee representatives" with (a),(b),(c) — acknowledged.

26. Final 351.905(e)(2)... proposal (f)(2): "No such stay may be ordered that would deprive pay and benefits to the employee" vs final "that would deprive the employee of pay and benefits" — wording only.

27. Final 351.909(b): adds rules for denial/dismissal — acknowledged.

28. Final 351.909(f)... acknowledged.

So the strongest Q14(ii) candidates: 
(a) 351.906(b) "shall" → "may" (mandatory to discretionary sanctions) — not in digest.
(b) 351.906 new (c) proportionality requirement — not in digest.
(c) 351.902(c)(2) addition of exemption clause "or exempted under paragraph (c)(7)" — not in digest.
(d) 351.901(c) removal of FLRA from preserved-entity list — not in digest (partially implied).
(e) 351.905(c) removal of "any other appropriate action"/direction to participate — not in digest.

Hmm, also compare 351.905(a): proposal "no OPM employee may be assigned to adjudicate an appeal if the employee ... was subject to, an action covered under this part" — final adds "during the preceding two years" scope and "shall be insulated...". Acknowledged in part ("Adding adjudicator-separation and ex parte safeguards"). Does digest acknowledge the two-year limit applying to "subject to an action" clause? Minor.

Also final 351.903(b)(1) provides "within 30 calendar days after service of the initial appeal" — same.

Also final 351.902(b): "An employee may submit an appeal... 30 calendar days from the effective date" same.

Also 351.907(a): proposal "Upon a request from either party"; final "Upon a request ... or upon its own initiative" — acknowledged.

OK. Now, I should also check the final's section-by-section (2279-3032) to find preamble statements that differ from text (Q14(i)). Let me grep within 2026-15666 for phrases like "part 351" / "this part" in the section-by-section? Better: read section-by-section portions for Subpart I (2349-3032) — ~680 lines, ~13k tokens. That's a lot but Q14 requires it. Alternatively grep for keywords: "sole and exclusive", "30 calendar days", "hearing", "burden", "agency record", "sanction", "MSPB".

Good. Note 351.901(c)(1) as published said "this part" — matching preamble; correction changed to "this subpart," creating mismatch with preamble at 49230, 49243, 49244, 49248, 49257.

Now, Q14(i) also: preamble at 2369-2374 says appellant must prove "the written appeal was timely and in the required form" while text (b)(1) says "the timeliness of the written appeal" — minor difference ("in the required form"). Also preamble 2386-2388 describes prejudice. Hmm.

Let me read section-by-section Subpart I (2349-3032) selectively — grep for text-quote-like statements. Perhaps I should read lines 2349-2560 and 2700-3032? That's heavy. Let me instead grep for specific numbers/provisions in that range via targeted patterns: "351.902", "351.905", "hearing", "30 calendar days", "agency record", "sanction", "MSPB".

Actually the more efficient approach for Q14(i): read the whole section-by-section for Subpart I (lines 2349-3032 = ~680 lines ≈ 13k tokens). I have 165k left and many questions still need reading (main rule preamble on E/G, 330.602 correction, admin leave rule, MSPB rule, proposed rule text for part 351 comparison (Q11), Q13 preamble-vs-text).

Q11 is potentially the biggest: compare proposed vs final part 351 regulatory text. I need the proposed rule's part 351 amendatory text (91 FR 10904). That's the bulk of the proposed rule (31 pages). Need to read it. And I have the final text already (mostly). The proposed text for part 351 subpart E, G, etc.

Budget plan (~165k remaining):
- Main final rule preamble Subpart E: ~12k (needed for Q2(c), Q5(a) old rules, Q4(e) modal rating, Q13).
- Main final rule preamble Subpart G: ~3k (Q6(e)).
- Main final rule preamble Subpart D/B/H: maybe 5k (Q9, Q13).
- Main final rule part 330 section + 330.602 text: 3k (Q10).
- 2026-18800: 2k.
- 2026-21320 (admin leave): 6k.
- 2026-16456 (MSPB): 5k.
- Proposal 2026-04377 part 351 text: 25k.
- 2026-15666 section-by-section: 10k.
- Q13 needs careful preamble reading: maybe 10k.

Total ~80k. OK feasible but tight. Let me move efficiently.

Next: read main rule preamble Subpart E (2253-2840).

  2253  D. Part 351, Subpart E: New Method of Deriving Retention Standing, 
  2254  Revised Order of Retention Examples, and Additional Examples
  2255  
  2256      OPM is finalizing its changes to 5 CFR part 351, subpart E 
  2257  ``Retention Standing,'' including revised and reorganized content in 
  2258  Sec. Sec.  351.501 through 351.504. In addition, OPM is renumbering 
  2259  current Sec.  351.505 Records and Sec.  351.506 Effective date of 
  2260  retention standing to Sec.  351.506 Records and Sec.  351.507 Effective 
  2261  date of retention standing, respectively.
  2262      As noted above, under this rule (and particularly Sec.  351.501 
  2263  Order of retention), when determining the order in which employees are 
  2264  placed on a RIF retention register, agencies will now do so based on 
  2265  whether the employee is in the competitive service tenure group or 
  2266  excepted service tenure group. Within each group, employees will be 
  2267  ranked based on performance, as augmented by additional points for 
  2268  veterans' preference. Where employees are tied, the employee in the 
  2269  higher tenure subgroup (with subgroup I ranked ahead of subgroup II) 
  2270  will be ranked ahead. When employees are still tied, the employee with 
  2271  the longer service will be ranked ahead.
  2272      In Sec.  351.502 Tenure of employment, OPM is redefining the tenure 
  2273  groups for both the competitive and excepted services. The competitive 
  2274  service tenure group will consist of all competitive service employees 
  2275  (in accordance with the provisions of Sec.  315.201) who are not (as of 
  2276  the date of the RIF notice) serving an initial probationary period or a 
  2277  temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less under 5 CFR 
  2278  part 316. The excepted service tenure group will consist of excepted 
  2279  service employees occupying a career position (as defined in Sec.  
  2280  213.101) who are not serving a trial period and are not serving in a 
  2281  temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less.
  2282      In addition, competitive service tenure subgroup I will include 
  2283  each career employee in the competitive service who, as of the date the 
  2284  employee receives a specific reduction in force notice, is not serving 
  2285  an initial probationary period. This definition is substantially the 
  2286  same as the current competitive service tenure group I.
  2287      Competitive service tenure subgroup II will consist of every other 
  2288  competitive service employee who, as of the date of the RIF notice, is 
  2289  not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary or term 
  2290  appointment of 1 year or less. For example, an employee serving under a 
  2291  career-conditional competitive service appointment who has completed a 
  2292  probationary period but not yet completed the service requirements for 
  2293  career tenure (under 5 CFR 315.201) would be included in subgroup II.
  2294      Excepted service tenure subgroup I will include all employees 
  2295  occupying a career position (that is to say, not in Schedule C or G) in 
  2296  the excepted service who, as of the date the employee receives a 
  2297  specific reduction in force notice, are not serving a trial period and 
  2298  whose appointment carries no restriction or condition such as 
  2299  conditional, indefinite, or specific time limit. This definition is 
  2300  substantially the same as current excepted service tenure group I.
  2301      Excepted service tenure subgroup II will consist of all other 
  2302  career employees in the excepted service (that is to say, not in 
  2303  Schedule C or G) who are not serving a trial period or a temporary or 
  2304  time-limited appointment of 1 year or less. Examples of employees in 
  2305  excepted service tenure subgroup II include employees occupying career 
  2306  positions in the excepted service who have completed any required trial 
  2307  period and who are serving under conditional, indefinite, or specific 
  2308  time-limited appointments of more than 1 year.
  2309      OPM revises Sec.  351.503 Performance to state that an agency will 
  2310  list employees on a RIF retention register (within the same tenure 
  2311  group) based on each employee's calculated performance credit. 
  2312  Generally, the three most recent ratings of record received during the 
  2313  4-year period prior to the date of issuance of reduction in force 
  2314  notices may be considered; however, an agency may establish a cut-off 
  2315  date after which no new rating of record will be considered. Ratings of 
  2316  record will be assigned a numerical value in conjunction with the 
  2317  patterns of summary level in 5 CFR 430.208(e) as follows:
  2318  
  2319  [[Page 49197]]
  2320  
  2321  
  2322

  2324                                                            Performance
  2325           Summary level            Rating description         credit
  2326  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2327  Level 5.......................  Outstanding or                         7

  2330                                   Successful or

  2335                                   Satisfactory or

  2337  Level 1.......................  Unacceptable.........                  0
  2338  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2339  
  2340      Agencies will list competing employees on the retention register in 
  2341  descending order (within the same tenure group) based on each 
  2342  employee's performance credit, which is the sum of the values assigned 
  2343  for their three most recent ratings of record received during the 4-
  2344  year period prior to the issuance of RIF notices. Employees would then 
  2345  receive additional performance credit based on veteran status: each 
  2346  preference eligible veteran with a compensable service-connected 
  2347  disability of 30 percent or more receives an additional 5 points added 
  2348  to their total performance credit, while every other preference 
  2349  eligible veteran would then receive an additional 3 points added to 
  2350  their total performance credit.
  2351      For example, the employees below are covered under a pattern C 
  2352  four-summary level rating performance appraisal system as described in 
  2353  5 CFR 430.208(e). Their ratings and totals are:
  2354  
  2355  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2356                                                                                      Performance
  2357                              Employee                                  Ratings         credit           Total
  2358  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2359  Alice...........................................................           5/4/4           7/5/5              17
  2360  Bill............................................................           4/3/3           5/3/3              11
  2361  Carol...........................................................           4/4/3           5/5/3              13
  2362  Fred............................................................           3/4/5           3/5/7              15
  2363  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2364  
  2365      These employees would be listed on the retention register in the 
  2366  following order: Alice, Fred, Carol, then Bill.
  2367      Section 351.503(b) Ratings used establishes which ratings of record 
  2368  may be used as the basis for calculating an employee's performance 
  2369  credit. For most employees, an employee's ratings of record are those 
  2370  recorded pursuant to subpart B of 5 CFR part 430.
  2371      Section 351.503(c) Consideration of performance includes language 
  2372  currently in Sec.  351.504(b) but modifies this language by removing 
  2373  the reference to ``additional retention service credit'' (i.e., credit 
  2374  for performance will no longer be added to an employee's length of 
  2375  service). Performance will now be the primary basis for rating 
  2376  employees within each tenure group. Performance will be measured based 
  2377  on performance credit, i.e., the total of each employee's summary level 
  2378  ratings for the employee's three most recent ratings of record for 
  2379  performance consistent with Sec.  351.503(a), which will then be 
  2380  augmented by additional credit for veterans' preference status as set 
  2381  forth in Sec.  351.504.
  2382      New paragraph Sec.  351.503(d) Single rating pattern describes how 
  2383  agencies list employees who have been covered under the same rating 
  2384  pattern of summary levels during the 4-year period prior to the date of 
  2385  issuance of the reduction in force notice or the agency-established 
  2386  cutoff date. Paragraph (d) provides that, for employees covered under a 
  2387  summary level appraisal system in which the highest summary level is a 
  2388  level ``3'' rating (i.e., a pattern A (`pass/fail'), or pattern D 
  2389  system authorized under 430.208(d) prior to the final rule prescribed 
  2390  at 91 FR 41521), the agency may, in its sole and exclusive discretion, 
  2391  give additional credit for employees who have documented exceptional 
  2392  performance to give more weight to certain performance-related actions 
  2393  than others for purposes of listing some level ``3'' employees ahead of 
  2394  other employees on a retention register. Evidence of exceptional 
  2395  performance may include documentation showing an agency has awarded: an 
  2396  employee with the highest Agency or Departmental award (such as a 
  2397  Secretary's or Chairman's award), a special act or service award, a 
  2398  quality step increase (QSI), or other performance awards or bonuses 
  2399  (e.g., a ``time-off'' award for demonstrated performance above 
  2400  expectations).
  2401      Commenter 0683 expressed concern that this could ``create[] a 
  2402  system in which the same level of actual performance could yield 
  2403  materially different retention outcomes depending on which agency the 
  2404  employee works for and what award budget was available.'' OPM 
  2405  disagrees. Instead, it believes this change will provide a method by 
  2406  which an agency may make meaningful distinctions among employees in a 
  2407  pattern A performance appraisal program (i.e., the highest summary 
  2408  level rating is a ``3'' or satisfactory) who have documented 
  2409  performance above expectations in these appraisal systems. It thus 
  2410  directly addresses Commenter 0683's concern that existing performance 
  2411  appraisal systems do not always meaningfully differentiate relative 
  2412  performance, along with Commenter 0683's concerns regarding variations 
  2413  in rating patterns across agencies.
  2414      For example, the employees below are covered under a three-summary 
  2415  level pattern as described in 5 CFR 430.208(e). Their agency has an 
  2416  established policy of providing enhanced performance credit by 
  2417  assigning 7 points for agency awards, 5 points for organizational 
  2418  awards, and 4 points for various performance awards. (An agency award 
  2419  is designated by ``A''; a component-level award is designated by ``O''; 
  2420  and a performance award or QSI is designated by ``P''.) Their ratings 
  2421  and totals are:
  2422  
  2423  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2424                                                                                    Assigned
  2425            Employee                Ratings       Performance       Award(s)       values for          Total
  2426                                                    credit                           awards
  2427  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2428  Carol.......................           3/3/3           3/3/3  O/O/A..........           5/5/7     3+3+3+5+5+7=26
  2429  Alice.......................           3/3/3           3/3/3  A/-/P..........           7/0/4       3+3+3+7+4=20
  2430  Bill........................           2/3/3           0/3/3  -/-/P..........           0/0/4     0+3+3+0+0+4=10
  2431

  2433  
  2434

  2436  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2437  
  2438      New paragraph Sec.  351.503(e) Multiple rating patterns addresses 
  2439  situations in which an agency has employees in a competitive area who 
  2440  have ratings of record under more than one pattern of summary levels, 
  2441  as described in 5 CFR 430.208(e). An agency may, in its sole and 
  2442  exclusive discretion, choose to provide enhanced performance credit to 
  2443  employees under disparate pattern summary levels. It may do so by 
  2444  transmuting or assigning an employee a higher summary level rating than 
  2445  what he or she received under a previous rating system when there is 
  2446  documented evidence of exceptional or higher-level performance 
  2447  consistent with the criteria in revised Sec.  351.503(d).
  2448      In addition, for an employee who goes from an appraisal system 
  2449  which uses a higher pattern of summary levels to a lower one (e.g., an 
  2450  employee who goes from a 5 summary level appraisal program to a two 
  2451  level system (i.e., pass/fail system)), an agency may adopt policies 
  2452  which would allow employees with ratings above the highest summary 
  2453  level of the lower pattern system to be listed ahead of any employee on 
  2454  the retention register who does not have documented evidence of 
  2455  exceptional performance as described above. This method allows agencies 
  2456  to adopt policies that would prevent exceptional performers from being 
  2457  disadvantaged because they may be covered under two or more patterns of 
  2458  summary rating levels which may not make meaningful distinctions for 
  2459  performance among employees. Further, Sec.  351.503 will require RIF 
  2460  performance ratings and assigned summary levels, including adjustments, 
  2461  to be uniformly and consistently applied within the competitive area 
  2462  and consistent with the agency's implementing issuances. Where an 
  2463  agency elects to assign additional performance credit, the agency must 
  2464  specify and document the criteria in advance and make them available 
  2465  for review.
  2466      Paragraph (f) of Sec.  351.503 describes how an agency should 
  2467  factor performance ratings into the RIF process when an employee does 
  2468  not have three actual ratings of record during the 4-year period prior 
  2469  to the date of issuance of RIF notices, or the 4-year period prior to 
  2470  the agency-established cut-off date. It uses the modal rating concept 
  2471  for employees with no ratings during the 4-year period prior to the 
  2472  RIF, as currently found in Sec.  351.504(c)(1), but modifies the 
  2473  current provisions by removing the reference to ``additional retention 
  2474  service credit.''
  2475      Section 351.504 Veterans' preference defines how veterans' 
  2476  preference will be applied in a RIF in both the competitive and 
  2477  excepted services. Each preference eligible employee with a compensable 
  2478  service-connected disability of 30 percent or more will receive an 
  2479  additional 5 points added to their performance credit, while every 
  2480  other preference eligible employee will receive an additional 3 points 
  2481  added to their performance credit. ``Preference eligibles'' is defined 
  2482  in 5 U.S.C. 2108(3) to include not only veterans, but also certain 
  2483  close family members of deceased or service-disabled veterans. Non-
  2484  preference eligible employees do not receive any additional points 
  2485  added to their performance score.
  2486      Commenter 0660 asserted, without any additional information, that 
  2487  ``the proposed rules are vague and unclear as to exactly how 
  2488  performance and veterans' issues are to be determined,'' but does not 
  2489  indicate in what manner the proposed rule is vague or unclear, 
  2490  providing no supporting information whatsoever. Commenter 0660 
  2491  contended that ``[t]he proposed regulation will make it likely that the 
  2492  classifications will result in numerous appeals challenging the order 
  2493  and create chaos in their implementation as a result,'' but failed to 
  2494  explain how the new regulation is more complicated than the current 
  2495  rules.
  2496      OPM disagrees with Commenter 0660's assertions. The current rules 
  2497  require agencies to categorize employees based on tenure group and 
  2498  veterans' preference subgroup. Employees are ranked first by tenure 
  2499  group I, II, III; then within each tenure group by veterans' preference 
  2500  subgroup AD, A, B; and only then by years of service as augmented by 
  2501  performance credit, starting with the earliest service date. Agencies 
  2502  then prepare an ``adjusted SCD'' calculation where extra years of 
  2503  service are added to an employee's actual service computation date. 
  2504  That means current RIF ordering is not a simple comparison of Employee 
  2505  A's performance against Employee B's performance. Agencies must first 
  2506  place employees into tenure groups, then veterans' preference 
  2507  subgroups, then calculate adjusted service dates. Performance affects 
  2508  ranking only inside the employee's already-determined tenure/veterans' 
  2509  preference category.
  2510      Agencies then must undergo multiple rounds of complicated bumping 
  2511  and retreating before arriving at a final retention register. Notably, 
  2512  ``bump and retreat'' can create a chain. If Employee A bumps Employee 
  2513  B, then Employee B is released from that competitive level, and the 
  2514  agency must determine whether Employee B has his or her own bump or 
  2515  retreat right. This process is highly burdensome and prone to errors.
  2516      This rule replaces the current rules with a streamlined system that 
  2517  eliminates the need for multiple, complicated rounds of bump and 
  2518  retreat, replacing it with a straightforward comparison of employee 
  2519  performance as augmented by veterans' preference, with ties broken by 
  2520  tenure and length of service. Further, OPM's new rules are simpler 
  2521  because they eliminate the most confusing features of the current 
  2522  rules: using performance to manufacture an adjusted service computation 
  2523  date and complicated bump-and-retreat procedures.
  2524      This rule addresses that problem by making performance credit more 
  2525  transparent and direct: Level 5 ratings receive 7 points, Level 4 
  2526  ratings receive 5 points, Level 3 ratings receive 3 points, and Level 1 
  2527  or 2 ratings receive no points. Veterans' preference is then added to 
  2528  that performance credit.
  2529      This rule's use of defined point values--Level 5 = 7 points, Level 
  2530  4 = 5 points, Level 3 = 3 points, and Level 1 or 2 = 0 points--also 
  2531  makes the RIF calculation easier to understand and audit than an 
  2532  artificial performance-adjusted SCD. As Commenter 0687 noted, this 
  2533  reform simplifies the composition of retention registers.
  2534      In addition, this rule does not change the basic record-keeping

Great: current rules described at 2496-2515: tenure group I,II,III; then veterans' preference subgroup AD, A, B; then years of service as augmented by performance credit, starting with earliest service date. Good for Q2(c)/Q5(a). Note: performance credit under old rules augmented SCD (adjusted SCD), but only inside the subgroup. So Bianchi (AD) above Abbott (B) regardless. And for Q5(a)(i): Lee and Park both subgroup B, tenure group I; performance credit adds to service credit: Lee's SCD 1998 with L3,3,3; Park's 2019 with L5,5,5. Under old rules, performance credit could add up to 3 years (per rating above fully successful? that's old 351.501(b) maybe: "20 years... additional credit of 1 year for each of the three most recent ratings of record at level 4 or above"?). Need to know: does the FR document describe how much credit? Maybe later in the preamble discussion or examples. Let's continue reading 2553-2840 which has examples that may include old-rules comparisons.

Also note the sentence at 2536: "this rule does not change the basic record-keeping requirements in current Sec. 351.505 (renumbered to Sec. 351.506) or the notice requirements in Sec. 351.802, except to conform..." — but the rule actually adds (c),(d),(e) to records? Actually those may already exist. Careful — Q13 asks about preamble statements that conflict with the text. Candidate: preamble at 2536 says notice requirements unchanged except conforming, while the rule changes 351.802(a)(2) to add "veterans' preference subgroup" and contents? Actually the other rule (appeals rule) amended (a)(6). Hmm, the main rule amended (a)(2) and (a)(3) — adding "veterans' preference subgroup" and "link to 5 CFR part 351" — which is more than conforming? Eh, arguably conforming to new subgroup structure. Not strong.

Let me continue reading 2553-2835.

content.text:
Differences spotted so far (proposed vs final, part 351):
1. 351.202(d)(1)(ii): proposed "An employee serving a trial period as of the date the agency issues a specific RIF notice" → final "An employee serving a trial period." Also (d)(1)(iii)/(iv) proposed "Schedule C appointments" / "Schedule G appointments" → final "An employee serving under a Schedule C appointment" (wording). Also (d)(2)(iii) proposed "temporary or term appointment of 1 year or less under subpart C or D of part 316" → final "temporary appointment of one (1) year or less under subpart D of part 316". That's substantive: term appointments ≤1 year removed and reference to subpart C removed. Also proposed (d)(3) "may be retained, furloughed, separated, demoted or reassigned without regard to the provisions of this part" → final (3) more detailed, plus new (4) notice requirement. Also final (d)(2)(i) says "An employee serving under an indefinite appointment who is serving an initial probationary period" (dropping "as of the date the agency issues a specific RIF notice").
2. 351.203 Furlough definition: proposed includes "and is instead dependent entirely on congressional action, rather than agency action" → final removed. Acknowledged in digest item 5 ("minor changes to the definition of 'emergency shutdown furlough'... to remove potentially confusing language").
3. 351.203 Rating of record: proposed "as specified in Sec. 430.208(d)" → final "as specified in Sec. 430.208(e))" — that's a citation change (not counted).
4. 351.203: proposed didn't add "Restoration protected employee" definition; final added it. Check: proposed instruction 19 list (a)-(k) does not include "Restoration protected employee"; final instruction 19 includes "Adding definitions in alphabetical order for 'Reduction in force', and 'Restoration protected employee'". So final ADDED a definition not in proposal — not acknowledged in the digest's list of changes from proposal (digest item 5 mentions only wording changes etc.). Hmm, digest item 1 mentions USERRA clarity; the restoration protected employee definition could fall under that. Risky. But it's a real addition to regulatory text; the summary item 1 discusses USERRA retention protections, which arguably covers it. I'd rather focus on clear ones.
5. 351.204: proposed lacks merit-system-principles sentence → final adds (acknowledged as item 2).
6. 351.303: same.
7. 351.402: proposed revised only (b); final revised (b) and (c) — final adds paragraph (c) requiring OPM submission when competitive area established/materially modified within 90 days. Acknowledged (item 3: additional competitive area safeguards). Though note digest item 3 says "submit a description of the competitive area and provide, for OPM review, a written explanation" while final text says "to OPM for approval in advance." Hmm — that's a Q13-type preamble/text mismatch ("for OPM review" vs "for OPM approval in advance"). Good candidate for Q13!
8. 351.502: proposed used "as of the date the agency issues a specific reduction in force notice" in (a)(2),(a)(3),(b)(2),(b)(3); final uses "as of the date the employee receives a specific reduction in force notice". That's substantive (issuance vs receipt) — and the final's digest item on retention standing mentions "fixes retention standing as of the date the employee receives a specific RIF notice (rather than the date the RIF is executed)" — doesn't acknowledge the change from "issues" to "receives" in the tenure definitions. Hmm, that's a Q11 item (proposed vs final). Also final (b)(3) fixed typo "all other employees in the occupying" → "all other employees occupying".
9. 351.503(a)(1): proposed "Level 2 (Minimally Successful or equivalent)" → final "Minimally Satisfactory". Also proposed cited Sec. 430.208(d) → final 430.208(e) (citation).

Continue reading proposed 3049-3370.

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty
